segments.narration: One violin sold for 15.9 million dollars in 2011. The Lady Blunt, built by Antonio Stradivari in Cremona in 1721.
He made over eleven hundred instruments. Around 650 still exist, and people have been chasing their secret for three straight centuries.
Dense wood from the Little Ice Age? Borax soaked in against woodworm? A varnish nobody could copy? Every theory got tested properly.
In 2010 the varnish came back as ordinary resin, oil and pigment. Nothing secret in it. So where is the magic hiding?
In 2014, ten soloists played twelve violins blind. Six picked a modern one, and guessing old from new came out roughly a coin flip. Thirty-one right, thirty-three wrong.

verdicts.claim: In the 2014 Fritz study ten soloists blind-tested six Old Italian violins including five Stradivari against six new ones, six of the ten chose a new violin, and their old-versus-new guesses were close to chance.
verdicts.note: The 2014 Fritz et al. PNAS study: ten soloists, six Old Italian violins (five Stradivari) against six new, two 75-minute sessions; 6 of 10 chose a new instrument, and old-versus-new guesses were 31 right to 33 wrong. Corroborated by Inside Science (AIP). Wikipedia lists the study and the general finding that blind tests find no reliable difference.
